name: Lena Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign for anything. What you say is confidential and won't be linked to your name. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a crew doing new connections on the edge of the city, where it's growing fast. New housing estates, a solar farm, a row of fast chargers for electric cars at a big roadside service station, and right now a big feeder line out to a data centre. I'm up at five thirty, I pray, I make the kids' lunches, and by six thirty I've used an AI assistant to shuffle the day's jobs around whatever the developers have messed up overnight. I love building something new where there was a field last year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You use AI to plan the day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I tell it which crews I've got, which jobs are ready and which roads are closed, and it gives me a plan in a minute that used to take me an hour with a whiteboard. I still make the final call, but it's like having a sharp assistant who never needs coffee. My husband Daniel jokes that I talk to my phone more than to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and the hype was overdone, which is usually how it goes. At work I'd keep showing people the tricks that save time. Online I'd maybe post in the trade group about how I plan my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means more of the same, and that's good. All these new estates and chargers still need connecting, so there's plenty of work. I'd keep my eye out for ways to grow, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and keep using the tools. Keep about three months saved and maybe push it to four. I'd also look at doing a short course on solar farm connections, because that's where the work's going anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew has picked up the tools from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, my second, he's thirty-five and was dead against it at first. Now he plans his own jobs with it and won't shut up about it. I think he just needed to see it work on a real day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep an eye out for ways to grow. What does growth mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More responsibility, more money for the family, and maybe one day something of my own. My dad ran a little hardware shop, and I grew up seeing what it means to build something. I'd like my kids to see that too.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are useful and the hype was overdone, as usual. I'd keep showing people time-saving tricks and post about it in the trade group.
S0.think: I think it means more of the same, which is good, because new estates and chargers keep the work coming. I'd still look for ways to grow.
S0.do: Keeps working and using AI tools, aiming to push savings from three months to four. Takes a short course on solar farm connections.
S0.quote: I think he just needed to see it work on a real day.
S0.fieldNote: Lena is a confident, enterprising crew lead who already teaches her crew to use AI. She sees growth, from housing to chargers to data centres, as plenty of work. Her father's hardware shop shapes her wish to build something of her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity for anyone willing to work for it. Learn the tools, take on more, and don't wait for someone to hand you a plan. That's what I'd say in the trade group and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I already use the tools daily and my area is growing. The only question is whether I stay an employee or start something myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a weekend business doing drone surveys for solar farms and new estates, probably with a second-hand drone for about two thousand. I'd push the company to put the new robot kit on my crew so we learn it first. And I'd keep saving, because a business can eat money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of a buzz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two thousand for a drone is a lot with three months saved. How would you and Daniel decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit at the kitchen table with a spreadsheet, like we did for the car. Daniel's careful, he works in a sheet-metal shop and measures everything twice. If the numbers worked, we'd do it, if not, we'd wait a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might struggle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older lads on the crew who don't like change. I'd try to bring them along, the way I did with Jonah. But in the end, people have to choose to learn.

S1.say: I'd say this is an opportunity for anyone willing to work for it: learn the tools, take on more and don't wait for someone to hand you a plan.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, since I already use the tools daily and my area is growing. The question is whether I stay an employee or start something myself.
S1.do: Starts a weekend drone survey business with a second-hand drone for about two thousand, if the numbers work. Pushes to get new robot kit on her crew first and keeps saving.
S1.feel: Calm with a bit of a buzz.
S1.quote: In the end, people have to choose to learn.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like a business chance to her. She and her husband plan money decisions together carefully, despite her taste for risk. She sees learning as a personal choice, which fits her outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock and families need to pull together. Don't wait for the government to save you, start planning tonight. And I'd say companies owe their people honest notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even being good with AI only buys me a little time. If a robot can build a line and an AI can plan it, they don't need me in either role. With three months saved and a mortgage, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any big spending straight away and push savings up as fast as possible. I'd try to set up something of my own quickly, maybe a company that installs and looks after the robots for local developers, using the contacts I've got. And I'd talk with Daniel about whether Marisol and Gabe need to change schools to save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but I'd feel it in my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said start planning tonight. What would you actually do that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pray, honestly, then get the spreadsheet out. Daniel and I would list every bill and every bit of income. Then I'd ring three developers I know and ask what they're planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marisol, who's twelve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That God hasn't left us, and Mum and Dad have a plan. I'd tell her to work hard at school and be kind, because those things last. I wouldn't tell her the numbers.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shock and families need to pull together and start planning tonight, not wait for government. Companies owe their people honest notice.
S2.think: I think being good with AI only buys me a little time, because robots and AI could do both my roles. With three months saved and a mortgage, it's frightening.
S2.do: Stops big spending and builds savings fast. Tries to quickly start a company installing and maintaining robots for local developers, and considers moving the children to cheaper schools.
S2.feel: Anxious, felt in her chest, but not frozen.
S2.quote: If a robot can build a line and an AI can plan it, they don't need me in either role.
S2.fieldNote: Even with her skills, she sees the fast picture as a real threat with thin savings. Her response is to pray, plan and start a business using her contacts. She'd shield her children from the money details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and anyone who wastes it has only themselves to blame. Learn, build, save. That's what I'd say to people at church and on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me. I could build a proper business on the side, installing and looking after robots and drones for developers and solar farms, and then go full time when the company starts cutting. I think I'd come out of it okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd register the business, buy the drone and do weekend jobs. I'd learn everything I can about the robot kit, maybe through the supplier's training. And I'd put any profit back into equipment instead of spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd feel ready to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who wastes it has themselves to blame. Isn't that hard on people with less choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it is, and I'd catch myself. Not everyone has my energy or a husband with steady work. I'd want churches and families helping those people, not just leaving them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when full AGI arrives in 2031, what happens to your business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question, and I don't fully know. I'd hope people still want someone they trust to look after their machines. If not, I'd have to think again at forty-eight.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a warning and anyone who wastes it has only themselves to blame. Learn, build and save.
S3.think: I think five years lets me build a business installing and maintaining robots and drones, then go full time when the company cuts. I'd come out okay.
S3.do: Registers the business, buys a drone and does weekend jobs in the first year. Learns the robot kit through supplier training and reinvests any profit in equipment.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly ready to go.
S3.quote: Not everyone has my energy or a husband with steady work.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her a clear business path, from weekend jobs to full time. When I pushed on her 'only themselves to blame' line, she softened and turned to churches and families for those with less choice. She admits she doesn't know what happens to the business once AGI fully arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Anyone can retrain or build something in ten years if they start now. Families and communities should be helping each other get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm confident. I'd build the business slowly and properly, maybe hire a couple of people from my crew. The kids would be through school by then, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business in year one as a weekend thing and grow it over five or six years. I'd invest in good equipment and maybe a small yard. I'd also talk to Marisol and Gabe about skills that last, like fixing things and dealing with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hire a couple of people from your crew, you said. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, definitely, he'd be great running the robot side. And maybe one of the older lads who knows every developer in the area. I'd want people I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel different from five, or is it just more of the same plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan, less rush. With five years I'd be stretching every weekend. With ten I could still go to Gabe's games.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone can retrain or build something if they start now. Families and communities should help each other get ready.
S4.think: I think I'd be confident with ten years, building the business slowly and maybe hiring people from my crew. The kids would be through school.
S4.do: Starts the business as a weekend venture and grows it over five or six years. Invests in good equipment and possibly a small yard, and talks with her children about lasting skills.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes her calm and excited, with the same business plan at a more family-friendly pace. She'd hire trusted colleagues. Her faith, family and entrepreneurial streak hold steady across all five scenarios.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because three months of savings doesn't last. What would help is honest notice from companies and simple, cheap loans for people starting small businesses, with less paperwork. And companies letting experienced people train on the new kit while they still have their jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what gives people purpose. A job's not just money, it's getting up and being useful. If the machines do everything, people still need somewhere to be useful, and that's families and churches as much as anything.

headlineQuote: I love building something new where there was a field last year.
portrait: Lena Garcia is a 43-year-old crew lead doing new connections on the fast-growing edge of a city, and she plans her day with an AI assistant every morning. She's faith-driven and enterprising, inspired by her father's small shop. She sees steady change as a chance to start a weekend drone survey business. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because three months of savings won't last, but she'd still pray, plan and try to start a business. With five or ten years she builds that business step by step, and the extra time mainly means less rush and more family time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because three months of savings wouldn't last.
whatWouldHelp: Honest notice from companies, simple cheap loans for small businesses with less paperwork, and training on new kit while people still have their jobs.
